summary: Defines how to carry Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) messages over secure CoAP instead of HTTPS. EST is a way for devices to get certificates, and CoAP is a lightweight protocol common on small, low-power devices. This lets constrained devices reuse existing EST functionality to obtain certificates.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9148 carries the certificate enrolment protocol, EST, over CoAP instead of over HTTP. CoAP is the lightweight protocol that small, low-power devices already speak, and DTLS protects it in the same way TLS protects HTTP. The enrolment messages stay the same; what changes is the transport, the shorter URLs and the binary payloads.

questions: how do iot devices get certificates
how do iot devices get certificates over coap
subtitle: How small, low-power devices get their certificates by running EST over secure CoAP instead of HTTPS.

tldr.problem: EST hands out certificates over HTTPS, but many Internet of Things devices speak the lightweight CoAP protocol instead of HTTP and cannot afford the full web stack.
tldr.mechanism: EST-coaps carries the same EST messages over CoAP secured with DTLS. It shortens the URLs, sends binary payloads instead of Base64, and uses CoAP block-wise transfer to split large messages.
tldr.outcome: Constrained devices can enroll for certificates with existing EST functionality. RFC 9148 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9908.

facts.label: Binary payload saving
facts.value: 30% smaller than Base64 for DER-encoded ASN.1

today: RFC 9148 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9908. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the specification of EST over secure CoAP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Classical Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST) of RFC 7030 is used for authenticated and authorized endpoint certificate enrollment, and optionally for key provisioning, through a Certification Authority or Registration Authority. EST transports its messages over HTTPS.

This document defines a new transport for EST based on the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP), because some Internet of Things devices use CoAP instead of HTTP. It therefore uses DTLS and CoAP in place of TLS and HTTP.

EST responses can be relatively large, so this specification also uses CoAP Block-Wise Transfer of RFC 7959 to offer a fragmentation mechanism for EST messages at the CoAP layer.

The document also profiles the use of EST to support certificate-based client authentication only. Neither HTTP Basic nor Digest authentication, as described in Section 3.2.3 of RFC 7030, is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: EST is how a device asks a certificate authority for a certificate. It normally runs over HTTPS, which is heavy for a small sensor. This RFC runs the same messages over CoAP with DTLS, and it adds a way to split a large reply into blocks so that no IP packet has to be fragmented.

sections.title: Security Profile and Authentication
sections.content:
EST-coaps can transport certificates and private keys. Certificates are responses to re-enrollment requests or to requests for a trusted certificate list, and private keys can be transported as responses to a server-side key generation request. The protocol depends on a secure transport that secures the exchanged CoAP messages, and DTLS is one such protocol. No other change is needed to the secure transport of EST messages.

In accordance with the profiles for low-resource devices in RFC 7925, the mandatory cipher suite for DTLS in EST-coaps is TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8. The curve secp256r1 must be supported, and it is equivalent to the NIST P-256 curve. DTLS 1.2 implementations must use the Supported Elliptic Curves and Supported Point Formats extensions of RFC 8422, and must also support the uncompressed point format. DTLS 1.3 implementations differ, because they do not support point format negotiation in favour of a single point format per curve, so support for DTLS 1.3 does not mandate the point format extensions, and the Supported Elliptic Curves extension has been renamed to Supported Groups.

CoAP was designed to avoid IP fragmentation. DTLS secures CoAP messages, but fragmentation is still possible at the DTLS layer during the handshake, and DTLS provides a mechanism for splitting a handshake message over a number of records that can each be transmitted separately, which avoids IP fragmentation.

The server is authenticated to the client by certificate authentication in the DTLS handshake, and the client must be configured with at least an Implicit Trust Anchor database, which lets it authenticate the server the first time, before it has an Explicit Trust Anchor. The client must be authenticated with a client certificate in the handshake, which can be a previously issued client certificate, for example one issued by the EST CA, or a previously installed certificate such as a manufacturer IDevID. IDevIDs are expected to have a very long life, as long as the device, but can expire under some conditions, and the server may then authenticate the client certificate against its trust store even though it has expired.

Connection-based proof-of-possession is optional. When it is wanted, a set of actions is required for the use of tls-unique, which consists of the contents of the first Finished message in the handshake. The client adds the Finished message as a challengePassword in the attributes section of the PKCS #10 certification request, to prove that it is in control of the private key at the time the session was established. For DTLS 1.3, where there is no equivalent of tls-unique, a 32-byte tls-exporter binding can be derived from the master secret and used in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: The security profile is fixed: one cipher suite is mandatory and one elliptic curve must be supported. The server proves who it is with a certificate, and the client must also present a certificate, either one it already got from this authority or one that came with the device. The client may additionally prove that it holds the private key for the key it is enrolling by putting a value from the handshake into the request.

sections.title: Discovery and URIs
sections.content:
EST-coaps is meant for low-resource networks with small packets. Two kinds of installation are possible: a rigid one, where the address and the supported functions of the EST server are known, and a flexible one, where the server and its functions have to be discovered. For both, saving header space matters, so this document specifies short EST-coaps URIs, which are shorter than those of RFC 7030, of the form coaps://example.com:<port>/.well-known/est/<short-est> and coaps://example.com:<port>/.well-known/est/ArbitraryLabel/<short-est>. Arbitrary labels are usually defined and used by EST certificate authorities to route client requests to the right certificate profile, and implementers should consider short labels to reduce transmission overhead. The URIs obtained through discovery have the form coaps://example.com:<port>/<root-resource>/<short-est>.

The mapping from the EST path to the short EST-coaps path is given in the table: /cacerts becomes /crts, /simpleenroll becomes /sen, /simplereenroll becomes /sren, /serverkeygen becomes /skg for a certificate in a PKCS #7 container or /skc for a single application/pkix-cert certificate, and /csrattrs becomes /att. Clients and servers must support the short URIs.

Discovery in CoAP is done by sending a GET request to /.well-known/core with a resource type parameter of ace.est*. The response lists the resources with their resource types, ace.est.crts, ace.est.sen, ace.est.sren, ace.est.att, ace.est.skg and ace.est.skc, and their content formats. The first three entries must be returned if the server supports resource discovery, and the last three are included only if the corresponding function is implemented. Discoverable port numbers can be returned in the response payload. The server must support the default /.well-known/est root resource, and should support resource discovery when it uses non-default URIs or ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The URLs are shortened so that a small device does not spend many bytes on them: /crts for the list of authority certificates, /sen and /sren for enrolling and re-enrolling, /skg and /skc for asking the server to make the key, and /att for the attributes to put in a request. A client that does not know the addresses asks the well-known core path with a resource type, and the server answers with the list of resources it offers and the formats it can produce.

sections.title: Functions and Payload Formats
sections.content:
The specification has a set of required-to-implement functions, optional functions, and functions that are not specified. The unspecified ones are deemed too expensive for low-resource devices in payload and calculation times: /cacerts, /simpleenroll and /simplereenroll must be implemented, /serverkeygen and /csrattrs are optional, and /fullcmc is not specified. While RFC 7030 permits several EST functions to be used without authentication, this specification requires that the client must be authenticated for all functions.

EST-coaps is designed for low-resource devices, so it does not need to send Base64-encoded data. Simple binary is more efficient, 30% smaller for DER-encoded ASN.1, and well supported by CoAP, so the payload for a media type follows the ASN.1 structure of that media type and is transported in binary form. The Content-Format option of CoAP takes the place of the HTTP Content-Type header and determines which EST message is carried in the payload, and the combination of URI path and Content-Format must map to an allowed combination of URI and media type in EST.

Content-Format 287 can be used instead of 281 to carry a single certificate rather than a PKCS #7 container in a /crts, /sen, /sren or /skg response. Format 281 must be supported by servers, and servers may also support 287, while the client may support only 281, only 287, or both, and expresses its preference with a CoAP Accept Option. If the request has no Accept Option, the client expresses no preference and the server should choose 281. Format 286 is used in the /sen, /sren and /skg requests, and 285 in the /att responses.

A representation with Content-Format 62 holds a collection of representations with their own content formats, and identifies the media type application/multipart-core. A server-side key generation response can therefore carry a private key in PKCS #8 with format 284 and a certificate in a PKCS #7 container with format 281, which in diagnostic CBOR notation looks like [284,h'0123456789abcdef', 281,h'fedcba9876543210'].
sections.plainLanguage: Three functions are required and two are optional, and every one of them needs the client to be authenticated. The payloads are sent as binary rather than as Base64 text, which is about 30% smaller for the DER-encoded structures that certificates use. A number of content formats tell the client and the server what a body holds, and a client can ask for a single certificate rather than a container of them.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Delayed Responses
sections.content:
DTLS defines fragmentation only for the handshake and not for the exchange of data records, and the records should be sized so that they fit within any path MTU estimate the record layer has obtained. That is not always possible in EST-coaps. Even with ECC, certificate sizes vary greatly with the signature algorithms, key sizes and object identifiers used: for 256-bit curves, common ECDSA certificate sizes are 500 to 1000 bytes, and for 384-bit curves they can sometimes reach 1.5KB. A response with the whole set of authority certificates can be larger still. CoAP gives good upper bounds of 1152 bytes for the message size and 1024 bytes for the payload size, and suggests that IPv4 implementations may want to limit themselves to 576 bytes. Even so, EST-coaps messages can exceed the path MTU, so the protocol has to be able to split them into several DTLS datagrams.

CoAP Block-Wise Transfer does that with the Block1 option for the request payload and the Block2 option for the response payload, and block-wise transfers should be used in Confirmable messages to avoid the exacerbation of lost blocks. Servers must implement Block1 and Block2, clients must implement Block2, and clients must implement Block1 only if they expect to send requests larger than the path MTU. The Size1 and Size2 options, which give size information about the representation, may be supported.

Server responses can sometimes be delayed. A slow server can acknowledge the request with an empty ACK and send the resource later. In particular, a slow server can answer an enrollment request with an empty ACK with code 0.00 before sending the certificate after a short delay, and if the certificate response is large it will need more than one Block2 block. The client sends the request in N1+1 Block1 blocks, the server announces the delayed response with an empty 0.00 ACK, and the response then arrives in 2.04 messages carrying N2+1 Block2 options, the first of which is Confirmable and is acknowledged by the client, and after which the client acknowledges each further block.

If the server is very slow, for example when a person has to approve the request, it should reply with an ACK carrying response code 5.03, service unavailable, and a Max-Age option giving the time the client should wait. After that delay the client should resend the identical request, and it keeps doing so for as long as the server answers 5.03 with a Max-Age, until the server returns the certificate or the client gives up.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates are often too big for one small packet, so the message is split into blocks and reassembled at the other end. The server may also need time to issue a certificate. When it does, it answers the request with an empty acknowledgement and sends the certificate later, or, if it needs minutes, it answers with a service-unavailable code and a waiting time, and the client repeats the request until the certificate is ready.

sections.title: Server-Side Key Generation
sections.content:
Private keys can be generated on the server, which suits cases where it is considered more secure to generate the long-lived random private key that identifies the client at the server, where the resources spent on generating a random private key at the client are scarce, or where the policy requires the certificate and key to be generated and controlled centrally.

When the client asks for server-side key generation, it asks the server or proxy to generate the private key and the certificate, which are transferred back in the response. The server treats the request as it treats any other enrollment request, with one distinction: it must ignore the public key values and the signature in the request. Those are included only so that existing code for generating and parsing such requests can be reused.

The /skg request is for a certificate in a PKCS #7 container and a private key in two application/multipart-core elements, while an /skc request is for a single application/pkix-cert certificate and a private key. The private key format the client wants is stated in the PKCS #10 request. If that request contains SMIMECapabilities together with DecryptKeyIdentifier or AsymmetricDecryptKeyIdentifier, the client expects format 280 for the private key, and the key is then encrypted symmetrically or asymmetrically as RFC 7030 describes. A request without SMIMECapabilities expects an unencrypted PKCS #8 private key with format 284.

The response is an application/multipart-core body containing a CBOR array with four items, and the two representations need not be in a particular order because each is preceded by its content format. The private key can be in unprotected PKCS #8 format, with format 284, or protected inside CMS SignedData, with format 280. The SignedData, in the outermost container, is signed by the party that generated the private key, which may be the EST server or the EST CA. Clients and servers that support server-side key generation must support unprotected PKCS #8 private keys, and should support the symmetric or asymmetric encryption of the key for deployments that need end-to-end encryption between the client and the server, such as when an entity between the client and the authority terminates the DTLS connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the device should not make its own key. The client asks the server to generate one, and the server ignores the key material in the request and returns a fresh key and its certificate instead. The key normally travels as plain PKCS #8, and can also be wrapped in a signed and encrypted container for deployments that need the key protected all the way to the client.

sections.title: The Registrar at the CoAP Boundary
sections.content:
In real deployments the EST server does not always sit inside the CoAP boundary. It can exist outside the constrained network, in which case it supports TLS and HTTP instead of CoAPS, and EST-coaps is used by the client inside the boundary while TLS carries the EST messages outside it. A Registrar at the edge is then required to operate between the CoAP environment and the external HTTP network.

The Registrar must terminate EST-coaps downstream and start EST connections over TLS upstream. It must authenticate, and optionally authorize, the client requests, and it must itself be authenticated by the EST server or CA. The trust relationship between the Registrar and the EST server should be established in advance, so that the Registrar can proxy the connections on behalf of several clients.

The proof-of-possession linking information is lost between the EST-coaps client and the EST server when a Registrar is present, because the Registrar terminates the DTLS connection and starts a new TLS connection with the authority. The EST server learns that a Registrar is present from its TLS client certificate, which includes the id-kp-cmcRA extended key usage extension. The EST server can then be configured to accept proof-of-possession information that does not match the current TLS session, because the authenticated Registrar is assumed to have verified it downstream.

The Registrar must follow the URI mappings and the response code mappings, and it must convert from CBOR major type 2 to Base64 encoding. If CMS end-to-end encryption is used for the private key, the encrypted blob must be converted at the Registrar to binary CBOR type 2 for the client, which is a format conversion that does not require decryption. Because large messages are fragmented into blocks, the Registrar must reassemble the blocks before translating the binary content to Base64 and relaying the message upstream. It must also support resource discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate authority often sits outside the small network, so something has to translate between the two worlds. That translator, the Registrar, ends the CoAP session at the edge of the constrained network and opens a TLS session to the authority. It checks the client, and the authority trusts the Registrar to be doing that on its behalf. One thing is lost in the translation: the proof that the client holds its own key can no longer be checked end to end, so the client has to trust the Registrar.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7030 are only partly valid here, because HTTP Basic authentication is not supported, so the advice about passwords does not apply. The rest of it continues to apply.

Modern security protocols need random numbers during the run, for nonces and for ephemeral key generation, and a device that generates its own key needs them too. A device that uses server-side key generation still needs locally generated random numbers, and the transport of keys generated at the server is inherently risky, so a deployment analysis should establish whether server-side key generation increases or decreases the probability of digital identity theft. The sources of randomness that laptops and desktops draw on, such as mouse movement or the movement of hard drive heads, are not available on many constrained devices, so other sources have to be used or dedicated hardware added.

It is recommended that the Implicit Trust Anchor database used for server authentication be managed carefully, to reduce the chance of a third-party authority with poor practices being trusted, and that it be disabled after the client has successfully received the list of authority certificates, which limits any weakness to the first exchange. Alternatively, when a /sen request immediately follows a /crts, a client may keep the connection authenticated by the Implicit Trust Anchor open for efficiency, but a client that interleaves other requests in the same DTLS connection should revalidate the server certificate chain against the updated Explicit Trust Anchor first, and should close the connection if the chain does not authenticate. Cipher suites whose names include _EXPORT_ and _DES_ must not be used.

In DTLS 1.2, including tls-unique in the certificate request links the proof-of-possession to the proof of identity, which implies but does not prove that only the authenticated client has access to the private key. The 3SHAKE attack poses a risk by letting an attacker who is on the path inject itself between client and server, even when channel binding is in use, so implementers should use the Extended Master Secret extension in DTLS. The specification still depends on tls-unique for DTLS 1.2, because a 3SHAKE attack does not expose the messages exchanged with EST-coaps, while DTLS 1.3 uses the tls-exporter binding instead, which avoids that risk. Interpreters of ASN.1 structures should take appropriate measures against invalid length fields, buffer overflows and malicious content.

The Registrar must be deployed with care, and only when direct client-server connections are not possible. It should be deployed only when direct connections are not possible, and the client should confirm that the server is acting as a registration authority by the presence of the id-kp-cmcRA extended key usage in the server certificate. In a server-side key generation case without end-to-end encryption, the Registrar may be able to see the private key, so the client has to put its trust in the Registrar.
sections.plainLanguage: The device needs a good source of random numbers, which small devices often lack. The list of trusted authorities has to be looked after, and the bootstrap trust should be dropped once the real list has arrived. The proof that the client holds its key is weaker than it looks in DTLS 1.2, and the RFC explains why that is acceptable here. And where a Registrar sits between the device and the authority, the device has to trust that the Registrar does its job.
